title: Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation
lead: Gravity strains our feet, pulls an apple from a tree and holds the Moon in its orbit, and Newton was the first to write it down in a form that holds everywhere in the universe. This section states his universal law of gravitation, gets the familiar acceleration of $9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$ out of it, turns it round to weigh Earth itself, and follows it out to the ocean tides, to the weightlessness of an astronaut in orbit and to the delicate experiment that fixed the gravitational constant.
objectives: Describe the gravitational effect of the Moon on Earth.
summary_html:
• Newton’s universal law of gravitation: Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force along a line joining them. The force is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. In equation form, this is $$\kF = G\frac{mM}{\kr^2},$$ where $\kF$ is the magnitude of the gravitational force. $G$ is the gravitational constant, given by $G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2\text{/kg}^2$.
  • Newton’s law of gravitation applies universally.
notes: Problems 2, 4, 6 and 8 have no answer in the book’s key and are left out.
exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags, weights and hints are AI-generated. Answers come from the book’s answer key; problems 2, 4, 6 and 8 (the accelerations at Earth due to the Moon and the Sun, the acceleration due to gravity at the surface of the Sun, part (b) of Example 6.6 re-solved with $\kac = \kv^2/\kr$, and the comparison of Neptune’s acceleration due to Pluto with its acceleration due to Uranus) have no keyed answer and are left out. The three AP items with no key—the circumstances that maximize the gravitational force, the mass of Titan, and the Sun’s field at Mercury against its field at Earth—are kept as open items with an AI-marked suggested approach rather than as graded choices, and the item that names “Equation 6.40” keeps the book’s wording and cites the passage that states the law. The four conceptual questions have no key and carry AI-marked suggested approaches. Section 6.4 prints the conceptual questions on action at a distance and on whether a satellite in orbit is in free fall word for word as this section prints them; gravity is introduced here, so both are kept here and 6.4 leaves its copies out. The conceptual question on the free body diagram of a satellite in an elliptical orbit is kept here because the single force it asks for is the gravitational attraction this section introduces; the change of speed it asks about is taken up by Kepler’s second law in Satellites and Kepler’s Laws: An Argument for Simplicity. Section 6.2’s problem on the percentage of the surface acceleration that gravity gives at an altitude of 300 km needs $\kg = GM/\kr^2$ from this section, but it has no keyed answer, so 6.2 leaves it out rather than holding it here.

figures.original_caption: Gravitational attraction is along a line joining the centers of mass of these two bodies. The magnitude of the force is the same on each, consistent with Newton’s third law.
The distance between the centers of mass of Earth and an object on its surface is very nearly the same as the radius of Earth, because Earth is so much larger than the object.

(a) Earth and the Moon rotate approximately once a month around their common center of mass. (b) Their center of mass orbits the Sun in an elliptical orbit, but Earth’s path around the Sun has “wiggles” in it. Similar wiggles in the paths of stars have been observed and are considered direct evidence of planets orbiting those stars. This is important because the planets’ reflected light is often too dim to be observed.

The Moon causes ocean tides by attracting the water on the near side more than Earth, and by attracting Earth more than the water on the far side. The distances and sizes are not to scale. For this simplified representation of the Earth-Moon system, there are two high and two low tides per day at any location, because Earth rotates under the tidal bulge. (a, b) Spring tides: The highest tides occur when Earth, the Moon, and the Sun are aligned. (c) Neap tide: The lowest tides occur when the Sun lies at 90º to the Earth-Moon alignment. Note that this figure is not drawn to scale.

Cavendish used an apparatus like this to measure the gravitational attraction between the two suspended spheres (m) and the two on the stand (M) by observing the amount of torsion (twisting) created in the fiber. Distance between the masses can be varied to check the dependence of the force on distance. Modern experiments of this type continue to explore gravity.

exercises.prompt: Jupiter has a mass approximately 300 times greater than Earth's and a radius about 11 times greater. How will the gravitational acceleration at the surface of Jupiter compare to that at the surface of the Earth?

answer.hint: The acceleration at the surface is $\kg = GM/\kr^2$, so compare the factor by which the mass grows with the square of the factor by which the radius grows.

exercises.prompt: Given Newton's universal law of gravitation (Equation 6.40), under what circumstances is the force due to gravity maximized?

answer.solution: $G$ is a constant and is thought to be the same everywhere in the universe, so nothing about it can be changed. The other two things the law names can be. In $\kF = GmM/\kr^2$ the force grows with the product of the two masses and falls with the square of the distance between their centers of mass, so the attraction is greatest when the two masses are as large as possible and the distance between them as small as possible. Because the distance enters as its square, closing the gap changes the force faster than adding mass does.

exercises.prompt: In the formula $\kg = \frac{GM}{\kr^2}$, what does G represent?

options: A gravitational constant that is the same everywhere in the universe
A gravitational constant that is inversely proportional to the radius
The factor by which you multiply the inertial mass to obtain the gravitational mass
answer.hint: The acceleration due to gravity is already on the left of the formula, and the section gives $G$ a measured value and calls it universal.

exercises.prompt: Saturn's moon Titan has a radius of $2.58 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$ and a measured gravitational field of $1.35\ \text{m/s}^2$. What is its mass?

answer.solution: The gravitational field at the surface of a body is $\kg = GM/\kr^2$, and here it is the mass that is wanted, so turn the relation round as the section does for Earth: $M = \kg\kr^2/G$. Everything on the right is given or known, so put in the measured field, the radius and the gravitational constant, $M = (1.35\ \text{m/s}^2)(2.58 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m})^2 / (6.674 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2)$, and the mass comes out in kilograms. This is the same calculation that gave an accurate value for Earth's mass once Cavendish had measured $G$.

exercises.prompt: A recently discovered planet has a mass twice as great as Earth's and a radius twice as large as Earth's. What will be the approximate size of its gravitational field?

answer.hint: In $\kg = GM/\kr^2$ the mass doubles, which doubles the field, and the radius doubles, which enters as its square.

exercises.prompt: Earth is $1.5 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m}$ from the Sun. Mercury is $5.7 \times 10^{10}\ \text{m}$ from the Sun. How does the gravitational field of the Sun on Mercury ($g_{\text{SM}}$) compare to the gravitational field of the Sun on Earth ($g_{\text{SE}}$)?

answer.solution: The field the Sun produces at a distance $\kr$ from its center is $\kg = GM/\kr^2$, and the same constant and the same solar mass appear in both cases, so the two fields differ only through the two distances. Take the ratio and everything but the distances cancels: $g_{\text{SM}}/g_{\text{SE}} = (r_{\text{SE}}/r_{\text{SM}})^2 = (1.5 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m}\,/\,5.7 \times 10^{10}\ \text{m})^2$. Mercury is the nearer of the two, so the ratio is greater than one and the Sun's field at Mercury is the stronger.

exercises.prompt: Action at a distance, such as is the case for gravity, was once thought to be illogical and therefore untrue. What is the ultimate determinant of the truth in physics, and why was this action ultimately accepted?

answer.solution: The ultimate determinant of truth in physics is observation. A statement about nature is accepted when what can be measured agrees with what it predicts, and no argument about whether it seems logical settles the matter one way or the other. Action at a distance seemed illogical because every force people were familiar with was exerted by contact, while gravity acts across empty space with nothing in between. It was accepted because Newton's law predicted what could be measured, and predicted it very well: one formula accounted for falling bodies and for the motion of the Moon, it gave the conic sections that moons, planets and comets were already known to follow, and the value of $G$ that Cavendish later measured between two ordinary masses in a laboratory is the value that works for the Moon and the planets as well. Later work has gone further and describes gravitation as the bending of space and time, but the law is kept because it agrees with observation.

exercises.prompt: Two friends are having a conversation. Anna says a satellite in orbit is in freefall because the satellite keeps falling toward Earth. Tom says a satellite in orbit is not in freefall because the acceleration due to gravity is not $9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$. Who do you agree with and why?

answer.solution: Anna is right. Free fall means that gravity is the only force acting, and that is exactly the case for a satellite in orbit: it keeps falling toward Earth while Earth's surface curves away beneath it, so it never arrives. Tom is applying the wrong test. The acceleration due to gravity is $\kg = GM/\kr^2$, and $9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$ is only its value at the distance of Earth's surface; further out the value is smaller, and the satellite falls with whatever value belongs to its own distance. That is also why the astronauts inside are weightless. They are in free fall along with the satellite, accelerating with the acceleration due to gravity, not beyond the reach of gravity, and there is no zero gravity in an orbit.

exercises.prompt: Draw a free body diagram for a satellite in an elliptical orbit showing why its speed increases as it approaches its parent body and decreases as it moves away.

answer.solution: Only one force acts on the satellite, the gravitational attraction of the parent body, so the free body diagram is a single arrow drawn from the satellite along the line joining the two centers of mass and pointing at the parent body. Draw the velocity arrow beside it at two places on the ellipse. On a circular orbit the force arrow is always at right angles to the velocity and can only turn the satellite, never change its speed. On an elliptical orbit the satellite is not always moving at right angles to the line joining the two bodies: while it is approaching, part of the force lies along the direction of motion and the speed grows; while it is moving away, that part of the force points backward along the motion and the speed falls. The angle between the two arrows in the diagram is what tells you which of the two is happening.

exercises.prompt: Newton’s laws of motion and gravity were among the first to convincingly demonstrate the underlying simplicity and unity in nature. Many other examples have since been discovered, and we now expect to find such underlying order in complex situations. Is there proof that such order will always be found in new explorations?

answer.solution: There is no proof of it. What Newton's laws of motion and gravitation showed is that a great many different things—a falling apple, our own weight, the orbit of the Moon, the paths of the planets and the comets—follow from one simple statement, and the same kind of unity has been found again and again since. That record is a very good reason to look for underlying order in a field nobody has explored yet, and it is why we expect to find it. But the expectation is drawn from experience rather than established as a theorem: the only thing that can show order in a new exploration is the observation and the measurement made there, and an exploration that found none would have to be reported as it stood.

exercises.prompt: Earth is not a perfect sphere. Its radius as well as the value of g vary with latitude. (a) Calculate Earth’s mass given the acceleration due to gravity at the North Pole is $9.807\ \text{m/s}^2$ and the radius of the Earth at the pole is 6356.8 km. (b) Compare this with the accepted value of $5.972 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}$.

answer.hint: Start from $\kg = GM/\kr^2$ and rearrange it for the mass, $M = \kg\kr^2/G$; the radius must be in meters.
answer.solution: a) $\kg = \frac{GM}{\kr^2} \Rightarrow M = \frac{\kr^2 \kg}{G} = 5.95296 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}$ b) This is slightly, but measurably, smaller than the accepted value, differing in the third significant digit. The equation we used to find g assumes a sphere, but we already noted that the radius at the pole is smaller than at the equator. The calculation gives the mass for a sphere of the radius we used—and ignores the additional mass outside that radius.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the Moon? (b) On the surface of Mars? The mass of Mars is $6.418 \times 10^{23}\ \text{kg}$ and its radius is $3.38 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$.

parts.hint: Use $\kg = GM/\kr^2$ with the mass and the radius of the Moon; both are in the tables of astronomical data.
The same relation with the mass and the radius the problem gives for Mars.

exercises.prompt: The Moon and Earth rotate about their common center of mass, which is located about 4700 km from the center of Earth. (This is 1690 km below the surface.) (a) Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration due to the Moon’s gravity at that point. (b) Calculate the magnitude of the centripetal acceleration of the center of Earth as it rotates about that point once each lunar month (about 27.3 d) and compare it with the acceleration found in part (a). Comment on whether or not they are equal and why they should or should not be.

parts.hint: Use $\kg = GM/\kr^2$ with the mass of the Moon and the distance from the Moon to the point 4700 km from Earth’s center.
The center of Earth goes round a circle of radius 4700 km once in 27.3 d, so $\kac = \kr\kw^2$ with $\kw = 2\pi/\kT$.

answer.solution:
a) $3.42 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m/s}^2$

b) $3.34 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m/s}^2$

The values are nearly identical. One would expect the gravitational force to be the same as the centripetal force at the core of the system.

exercises.prompt: (a) Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted on a 4.20 kg baby by a 100 kg father 0.200 m away at birth (he is assisting, so he is close to the child). (b) Calculate the magnitude of the force on the baby due to Jupiter if it is at its closest distance to Earth, some $6.29 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m}$ away. How does the force of Jupiter on the baby compare to the force of the father on the baby? Other objects in the room and the hospital building also exert similar gravitational forces. (Of course, there could be an unknown force acting, but scientists first need to be convinced that there is even an effect, much less that an unknown force causes it.)

parts.hint: Put the two masses and the separation straight into $\kF = GmM/\kr^2$.
The same relation with the mass of Jupiter and the distance given; the mass is very much larger and so is the distance.

parts.part: (b) the ratio of the father’s force to Jupiter’s
parts.hint: Divide the force in (a) by the force in (b).

exercises.prompt: (a) The Sun orbits the Milky Way galaxy once each $2.60 \times 10^{8}\ \text{y}$, with a roughly circular orbit averaging $3.00 \times 10^{4}$ light years in radius. (A light year is the distance traveled by light in 1 y.) Calculate the centripetal acceleration of the Sun in its galactic orbit. Does your result support the contention that a nearly inertial frame of reference can be located at the Sun? (b) Calculate the average speed of the Sun in its galactic orbit. Does the answer surprise you?

parts.hint: Turn the radius into meters and the period into seconds, then use $\kac = \kr\kw^2$ with $\kw = 2\pi/\kT$.
The circumference of the orbit divided by the period, or $\kv = \kr\kw$.

exercises.prompt: Unreasonable Result A mountain 10.0 km from a person exerts a gravitational force on him equal to 2.00% of his weight. (a) Calculate the mass of the mountain. (b) Compare the mountain’s mass with that of Earth. (c) What is unreasonable about these results? (d) Which premises are unreasonable or inconsistent? (Note that accurate gravitational measurements can easily detect the effect of nearby mountains and variations in local geology.)

parts.hint: Set $GmM/\kr^2$ equal to $0.0200\,m\kg$; the person’s mass cancels, leaving the mass of the mountain.
Divide the mass found in (a) by the mass of Earth.

answer.solution:
a) $2.937 \times 10^{17}\ \text{kg}$

b) $4.91 \times 10^{-8}$ of the Earth’s mass.

c) The mass of the mountain and its fraction of the Earth’s mass are too great.

d) The gravitational force assumed to be exerted by the mountain is too great.
